client: I've been really struggling lately with my thesis deadlines kind of sneaking up on me, and I honestly don't know how I'm managing to keep everything together between that, my part-time job, and trying to maintain some kind of social life. It feels like no matter what I focus on, something else is falling apart, and the anxiety just keeps building. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because at the end of the day the deadlines are still there and I still have the same number of hours in a day.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now, and that constant sense of something slipping through the cracks must be exhausting — it makes complete sense that the anxiety keeps building. I also notice you came here even while doubting it would help, which tells me a part of you is still looking for a way through this. I'm curious — when you imagine everything "falling apart," what does that actually look like to you, and how likely do you feel that is to truly happen?

client: Yeah, when I picture it falling apart, I see myself losing my job because I keep missing small things — like forgetting to follow up on an email or spacing out in a meeting — and then I can't pay rent, and I end up completely alone with no one to turn to. I know logically that's a pretty extreme jump, but in the moment it feels like one small mistake is already the first domino falling. And honestly, the fact that I'm even here feels a little embarrassing, like I shouldn't need this much help just to function.
therapist: That image of the falling dominoes is such a vivid way to describe how anxiety works — it takes one small, real thing and fast-forwards it to the worst possible ending, skipping over all the steps where you'd actually have choices and resources along the way. And I want to gently push back on the embarrassment piece: the fact that you're juggling a thesis, a job, and a social life while still self-aware enough to seek support isn't a sign of weakness — it's actually evidence of someone trying really hard to cope. When you think about the "missed email" or "spacing out" moments, what has actually happened as a result of those so far?

client: Honestly, when I actually think about it... nothing catastrophic has happened yet. Like, my advisor hasn't pulled me aside, I haven't lost my job, my friends haven't stopped texting me. But it almost feels dangerous to admit that out loud, like I'm tempting fate or something, and my brain immediately jumps to "well, it's only a matter of time."
therapist: What you just did there is actually really significant — you looked for the evidence and found that reality is telling a very different story than your anxiety is. That feeling of "tempting fate" is a common way our anxious minds protect the worry itself, almost like the anxiety has a vested interest in not being questioned. I'm wondering — if a close friend described exactly your situation to you, same workload, same small slip-ups, same outcomes so far, would you tell them it's "only a matter of time" before everything collapses?

client: Honestly... no, I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably tell them they're doing fine and that a few small mistakes don't define everything. But it feels different when it's me — like I don't deserve the same kind of understanding I'd give to someone else, and I'm not sure why that is.
therapist: That gap you just noticed — between the compassion you freely give others and the harshness you turn on yourself — is such an important thing to name, and it's something a lot of people struggle with without ever quite seeing it so clearly. It's worth sitting with the fact that you didn't hesitate to extend kindness to your imaginary friend, which means that generosity *is* in you — it's just not being aimed in your direction yet. What do you think you might be protecting yourself from, if you started treating yourself with that same understanding?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think maybe... if I started being kind to myself, I'd have to admit that I actually deserve it, and then I'd have to face how long I've been treating myself like I don't. It feels safer to stay in the harshness, like at least I know what to expect there.
therapist: What you just said takes real courage to recognize — that the harshness feels like familiar ground, almost like a strange kind of safety, even while it's quietly costing you so much. That insight, that self-criticism has been a coping strategy rather than the truth about your worth, is actually a really meaningful place to arrive at. I'm curious — when you think back, is there a sense of where you first learned that being hard on yourself was the "safer" way to be?

client: I think it goes back to when I was a kid, honestly. My parents weren't cruel or anything, but there was this unspoken rule that if you criticized yourself first, you kind of beat everyone else to the punch, and it hurt less that way. Like if I already knew I was the problem, no one could surprise me with it.
therapist: That makes so much sense — you learned something really adaptive as a child, that getting there first meant you could control the pain a little, and that was genuinely clever survival at the time. But it sounds like that strategy has quietly followed you into adulthood, where it's no longer protecting you from anything real, just costing you the kindness you actually deserve. I'm wondering — now that you can see it for what it is, a learned habit rather than a truth about you, does it feel any different to sit with that self-criticism when it shows up?

client: I mean... yeah, it does feel a little different when you put it that way, like it's not just who I am but something I picked up along the way. But honestly, even knowing that doesn't make it stop — the voice is still just as loud, still just as convincing in the moment. I guess I'm not sure how understanding where it came from actually helps me when I'm in the middle of it and it feels completely real.
therapist: You're naming something really important — insight alone doesn't automatically turn down the volume, and it would be frustrating if I suggested that understanding it was enough to fix it. But here's where that knowledge actually becomes useful: in the middle of that loud, convincing moment, even a tiny pause to think "this is an old habit trying to protect me, not the truth" can create just enough space to choose a different response, even slightly. What do you think it might look like to experiment with that — not silencing the voice, but just gently questioning it once, the next time it shows up?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I guess the idea of just questioning it once feels less overwhelming than trying to shut it down completely. But honestly, in those moments when the anxiety hits and I'm convinced I've done something wrong or hurt someone, it's like my brain goes into this tunnel vision and I can't think clearly at all. I'm not sure I'd even remember to pause, let alone question anything — it just takes over so fast.
therapist: That tunnel vision you're describing is so real — when anxiety floods in that fast, it's genuinely hard to access the thinking part of your brain in the moment, and it's not a personal failing that it feels impossible to pause mid-spiral. This is actually why it helps to practice the pause *before* the tunnel arrives — even something as small as a phrase you decide on now, like "this is the old habit," that you've already committed to memory, so it's there waiting rather than something you have to construct under pressure. What's a simple, honest phrase that might feel true enough to you that you could actually reach for it in that moment?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I get the logic of having something ready in advance. But I'm honestly not sure what phrase would feel true enough — like, if I say something to myself that feels even slightly hollow, I think my brain would just reject it immediately and make things worse. Maybe something like "this feeling has passed before" could work, but even as I say it, I'm not totally convinced I'd believe it in the moment.
therapist: "This feeling has passed before" is actually a really grounded choice — it's not asking you to feel okay or dismiss the anxiety, it's just pointing to something your own history has already proven true, which makes it much harder for that skeptical part of your brain to argue with. The fact that you're already anticipating how your mind might reject something hollow shows real self-awareness, and that same discernment is what makes this phrase a stronger candidate than something more cheerful or forced. I'm curious — can you think of a specific recent moment when that anxious tunnel vision did eventually lift, something concrete you could hold onto as the proof behind those words?

client: I mean... yeah, there was last Thursday when I was convinced I'd completely bombed a presentation at work and spent the whole morning just spiraling about it. By the afternoon I got some positive feedback and the whole thing kind of dissolved, but in the moment it felt so permanent, like it would never lift. I guess that's a real example, but part of me worries that remembering it in the middle of a panic won't actually work — like my brain will just say "that was different" and dismiss it.
therapist: Last Thursday is actually a really powerful piece of evidence precisely because it was so recent and so visceral — your brain predicted permanence, and reality proved it wrong, and that's not a small thing. You're right that your mind might try to say "that was different," and honestly, it probably will, because that's what anxious minds do — but the goal isn't to win that argument, just to slow it down enough to create a little breathing room. What do you think it would mean for you if, even once, you managed to ride out that tunnel vision with "this feeling has passed before" and it actually helped, even just a little?
